note: Bare fetch() call sites with a non-constant URL. Seeded from the state on 2026-08-10 so the gate can only ratchet down. A new one must either use safeFetch (utils/url-validator.ts) or be added here with a reason. The federation entries are the documented carve-out. FULLY TRIAGED 2026-09-13: every entry now says what makes that call site right, and none carries the seeding placeholder any more. Two calls were moved rather than cleared (the work-expiry webhook, which fired a caller-supplied callback_url with no redirect re-validation, and the work forward to a remote node, which validated one hop and then followed any number), and eighteen entries were deleted because the scanner learned to skip comments on 2026-08-15 and nobody re-read the file afterwards: they pointed at prose. Adding an entry means writing what a reader can check, and it answers ONE question: can a low-privilege principal steer this address. Re-seeding forgives the whole file and is the developer's decision, never maintenance.

Same ruling and guard as the sibling entries: ai-completion.ts:499 calls assertProviderAllowed(config, baseUrl) before decrypting the key, and baseUrl is the owner's own reserved-prefix setting. NOTE for whoever reads this next: the allowlist is only a confinement when the operator configured one, because assertProviderAllowed returns immediately on an empty list, and an empty list is the default. That is the deliberate shape — an owner may point their own model calls at their own machine — not an oversight. Reviewed 2026-09-13.

This one IS reviewed, unlike its three seeded siblings above. `baseUrl` comes from the owner's own openrouter.settings and is checked against config.aiProviderAllowlist by assertProviderAllowed() BEFORE the key is decrypted, so a low-privilege principal cannot steer it: an app-grant token cannot write the reserved openrouter.* prefix at all. safeFetch is the wrong tool here for a positive reason too, since it blocks private addresses and a node running a local model server points at one deliberately.

The owner's own provider endpoint, same as its siblings, and reviewed with one difference recorded rather than waved past: this one's two callers, routes/openrouter.ts:396 and routes/llm-proxy.ts:79, do NOT call assertProviderAllowed, while every completion, image and transcription path does. On a node whose operator configured an allowlist, listing models therefore reaches a host the allowlist would refuse. It is the owner's own baseUrl and the owner's own key either way, so nothing crosses between people, and on a default node (empty allowlist) the two paths already agree. Left as a named inconsistency for the developer rather than closed here, because tightening it changes what an operator's allowlist does to a working feature. Reviewed 2026-09-13.
